title: Value Booster: Why Are You Here?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart draws on Ayelet Fishbach's Get It Done to explain research by psychologist Kentaro Fujita showing that people who reflect on goals by answering "why" questions become more motivated and work harder than people who answer "how" questions about the same goals. He connects this to Fishbach's broader claim that concrete goals feel like chores while abstract, purpose-driven goals feel meaningful, and links it to the Value belief in his five-key-beliefs framework and to Chris Hulleman's Build Connections intervention research. The practical takeaway is a single question teachers can ask any student, motivated or not: "Why are you here?" Stuart frames student-generated value signaling as more durable than teacher-generated value signaling because it travels with students after they leave the classroom.
points: Fujita's research found that answering "why" questions about a goal increases motivation and effort (measured via handgrip strength) compared to answering "how" questions about the same goal.
Stuart connects the why/how distinction to his Value belief: abstract, purpose-driven framing of a goal feels meaningful, while concrete framing feels like a chore.

Student-generated value signaling is more resilient than teacher-generated signaling because students carry their own answers with them after leaving the classroom, unlike teacher explanations of a subject's beauty.
The concrete classroom move is simple: ask a student, starting with a motivated one, "Hey — why are you here?" and genuinely listen before trying it with less-motivated students.
quotes: After answering several such questions, the research participants started to think about their goals either more abstractly [the WHY group] or more concretely [the HOW group] depending on the series of questions they'd answered. Those who answered a series of 'why' questions were more motivated to channel resources to their goals.
Telling someone that "I maintain good physical health so that I can be a more energetic father" does something to your heart that telling someone "I run three times per week" just doesn't do.

My take is that the WHY question format activates the Value belief in the hearts of participates. This kind of makes sense when you compare the Fujita experiment above with one I wrote about in These 6 Things.

The student-generated kind is, of course, the more resilient — this is why Hulleman's studies end up yielding results years after the intervention. When my students leave my classroom at the end of the year, I don't travel along on their shoulders, daily explaining the beauty of an education.
Your first goal? To listen and understand the hearts of the people you teach. Your second goal? Who knows — maybe they'll start holding the handgrip a little harder tomorrow.
